trial_name: ALBIOS — Albumin Replacement in Patients with Severe Sepsis or Septic Shock (2014)
citation: Caironi P, Tognoni G, Masson S, Fumagalli R, Pesenti A, Romero M, et al. Albumin replacement in patients with severe sepsis or septic shock. N Engl J Med. 2014;370(15):1412-1421
one_liner: Protocolised 20% albumin replacement to target serum albumin ≥30 g/L alongside crystalloids did not reduce 28-day or 90-day mortality in severe sepsis or septic shock.

pico.population: Adults (≥18 years) admitted to ICU within 24 hours of meeting severe sepsis or septic shock criteria.
pico.intervention: 20% albumin solution added to crystalloids, dosed daily to target serum albumin ≥30 g/L for up to 28 days or ICU discharge.
pico.comparison: Crystalloids alone for volume replacement using identical hemodynamic targets.
pico.outcome: Primary outcome was all-cause mortality at 28 days; key secondary outcome was 90-day mortality.

background.existing_knowledge: Colloids, including human albumin, were widely used in sepsis for intravascular volume expansion, but clinical outcome superiority over crystalloids remained unproven. The SAFE trial found no overall mortality difference, though a pre-specified severe sepsis subgroup suggested possible benefit.
background.knowledge_gap: Whether targeted, sustained correction of hypoalbuminemia using hyperoncotic 20% albumin improves survival and organ function in severe sepsis and septic shock.
background.hypothesis: Targeted 20% albumin replacement to maintain serum albumin ≥30 g/L in addition to crystalloids reduces 28-day mortality compared with crystalloids alone.

methods.design: Multicenter, open-label, randomized controlled trial stratified by ICU and time from meeting severe sepsis criteria (<6 hours vs 6–24 hours).
methods.setting: 100 ICUs across Italy; enrolled patients meeting Sepsis-1 severe sepsis/septic shock criteria within prior 24 hours.

inclusion: Meeting criteria for severe sepsis or septic shock within the prior 24 hours
exclusion: Known contraindication or allergy to albumin
Consent constraints or other protocol-specified exclusions

methods.intervention: 20% albumin plus crystalloids to maintain serum albumin ≥30 g/L daily for up to 28 days or ICU discharge.
methods.comparison: Crystalloids alone for fluid replacement; albumin and other colloids discouraged except for defined exceptions.
methods.sample_size_power: 1350 patients originally planned for 80% power at alpha 0.05 to detect a 17% relative risk reduction in 28-day mortality (45% to 37.4%); sample re-estimated at interim analysis up to 1818 participants.
secondary_outcomes: ICU and hospital length of stay
methods.follow_up: 28 days for primary outcome; 90 days for long-term survival.

headline_bullets: No difference in primary outcome of 28-day mortality (31.8% vs 32.0%; RR 1.00; P=0.94).
No difference in overall 90-day mortality (41.1% vs 43.6%; RR 0.94; P=0.29).
Albumin achieved biological separation (higher serum albumin and 6-hour MAP) and faster vasopressor weaning (median 3 vs 4 days; P=0.007).
Septic shock subgroup showed a univariable 90-day mortality reduction (RR 0.87; P=0.03) that attenuated after full adjustment (RR 0.88; P=0.07).

outcomes_table.note: Tertiary outcome; susceptible to open-label bias
Direction toward more RRT with albumin

outcomes_table.outcome: Serum albumin at day 1 (g/L; mean ± SD)
Mean arterial pressure at 6 hours (mmHg; mean ± SD)
Net fluid balance at day 2 (mL; median [IQR])
outcomes_table.note: Total 7-day net balance did not differ (P=0.13)

outcomes_table.outcome: Total administered fluids over 7 days (mL; median)
outcomes_table.note: Total crystalloids over 7 days: 14150 vs 16160 mL (P=0.07)

outcomes_table.outcome: Packed red blood cell volume (mL; median [IQR])

subgroup_table.subgroup: Septic shock at enrolment (90-day mortality, adjusted)
No septic shock at enrolment (90-day mortality)

safety: No statistically significant difference in AKI incidence (21.9% vs 22.7%; P=0.71).
No statistically significant difference in RRT use (24.6% vs 21.4%; P=0.11), though non-significantly higher in albumin group.
Higher PRBC transfusion volumes observed in albumin arm (median 600 vs 300 mL; P<0.001).

domains.notes: Central computer-generated sequence stratified by ICU and enrolment timing; allocation concealment adequate.
Open-label design; mortality is objective, but subjective outcomes like vasopressor weaning are vulnerable.
Minimal loss to follow-up (28-day mortality available in 895/903 vs 900/907 patients); ITT analysis performed.
High noncompliance: 41.8% in albumin arm were noncompliant at least once; 37.1% of crystalloid controls received albumin; synthetic colloids used in 22.7% vs 23.6%.
Well balanced: median age 70 vs 69 years, female sex 39.9% vs 39.4%, median SAPS II 48 vs 48.

internal_validity.verdict: Internal validity is moderate, limited by open-label design, high protocol noncompliance, and substantial control group crossover.

domains.notes: Broad adult ICU severe sepsis and septic shock cohort across 100 ICUs, but reflects Sepsis-1 definitions.
Requires daily serum albumin monitoring and hyperoncotic 20% albumin access, which is costly and resource-intensive.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is fair for modern practice, constrained by changing sepsis definitions and intervention resource requirements.

strengths: Pragmatic population with high baseline illness severity
Achieved clear biochemical and hemodynamic separation
limitations: Open-label design introducing performance bias risk
Substantial control group contamination (37.1% received albumin)
Lower baseline mortality than assumed (32% vs 45%), reducing statistical power
Subgroup findings vulnerable to multiplicity and residual confounding

critical_appraisal.summary: ALBIOS is a large, well-designed RCT showing that correcting hypoalbuminemia does not reduce mortality, though significant contamination biased results toward the null.
strengths: Rigorous central randomization and complete follow-up for primary endpoint
Clear biochemical proof of target achievement
weaknesses: Open-label administration leading to co-intervention imbalances
High crossover and noncompliance rates in both arms

sections.authors_conclusion: In patients with severe sepsis or septic shock, replacement of albumin in addition to crystalloids to maintain a serum albumin level of 30 g/L or more did not improve survival at 28 or 90 days.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Does not support routine targeted albumin replacement to maintain serum albumin ≥30 g/L in sepsis.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with severe sepsis or septic shock.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean albumin is harmful or entirely ineffective as an adjunct in severe septic shock requiring massive crystalloid volumes.
implementation_caveats: Crystalloids remain standard first-line resuscitation fluid.
Albumin can be considered conditionally when large crystalloid volumes are needed.
Targeting a specific serum albumin level (≥30 g/L) adds cost without survival benefit.

controversies.topic: Targeted replacement vs resuscitation fluid choice
controversies.notes: ALBIOS evaluated sustained correction of hypoalbuminemia rather than hyperoncotic albumin as an initial resuscitation bolus.
37.1% of control patients received albumin, which likely attenuated treatment differences toward the null.
Univariable 90-day survival benefit in septic shock (RR 0.87; P=0.03) lost significance after full covariate adjustment (RR 0.88; P=0.07).

context_related_trials.relation: SAFE evaluated 4% albumin vs saline for ICU fluid resuscitation and found severe sepsis subgroup benefit, inspiring the ALBIOS trial.

unresolved_questions: Does early hyperoncotic albumin resuscitation specifically benefit patients in refractory septic shock requiring high vasopressor doses?
What exact threshold of crystalloid volume marks the point where switching to albumin improves outcomes?

numbers_to_remember: Septic shock 90-day mortality subgroup 43.6% vs 49.9% (RR 0.87; P=0.03)
quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Targeted 20% albumin replacement to maintain serum albumin ≥30 g/L does not improve 28- or 90-day survival in sepsis, reinforcing crystalloids as primary resuscitation fluid.
